newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BHF-Bank H1 profit lags rivals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BHF-Bank H1 profit lags rivals.

text.p: BHF-Bank AG, the German investment bank often touted as a takeover target, on Wednesday posted a below-par rise in first-half operating profit and predicted satisfactory full-year earnings.

BHF-Bank said group operating profit after loan loss provisions rose 9.5 percent to 162 million marks ($88.1 million), lagging behind Germany's top commercial banks like Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank which have reported double-digit income gains.
Pre-tax profit rose 10.4 percent to 181 million marks.

Earnings were driven by a 14.4 percent rise in commission income to 246 million marks amid booming stock markets while net interest income stagnated, rising 0.8 percent to 358 million marks, BHF said.
"Building on the business revival in the first half we expect our commission business to remain positive," BHF said.
It added: "In view of moderate cost growth we are confident of being able to reach a satisfactory overall profit provided that markets remain good."
BHF-Bank's shares fell 1.90 marks on the news to close floor trade at 57.60 marks, underperforming the DAX index of 30 leading shares which rose almost one percent.
The shares have surged more than 60 percent since January amid takeover rumours which most recently focused on a possible acquisition by Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG.

One of Germany's 10 largest banks, BHF-Bank is well positioned in the domestic corporate banking scene with good links to the Mittelstand, or medium-sized businesses, and would offer a buyer a good foothold in Germany's main financial centre, Frankfurt.
UBS is believed to have taken a look at it and other Swiss and Dutch banks are also regarded as potential predators.

BHF has emerged from a difficult 1996. Its operating profit fell five percent last year as earnings were hit by a dividend omission from industrial holding group AGIV AG, of which BHF owns just under 50 percent.
The bank said on Wednesday progress had been made in the restructuring of AGIV which led to the formation of substantial hidden reserves in its stake since the end of 1996.
Net risk provisions rose 5.9 percent but the bank said it did not expect the need for provisioning to be as high in the full year 1997 as in 1996.

Administration costs rose 5.0 percent to 421 million marks. Own-account trading income fell 5.0 percent to 57 million marks but rose substantially if non-realised trading income is included, BHF-Bank said.
The balance sheet total rose to 79.7 billion marks at end-June from 74.1 billion at end-December. Lending rose 6.6 percent to 63.9 billion marks.
